\begin{bankq}[id=TOAS11-P1-CHEM-S2-Q06, source={TOAS - Test 11 (27 Jun 2022)}, paper=1, qno=6, type=multi, subtopic={Orbitals}, answer={A,B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=2, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: hydrogen-like wave function | steps: identify n and l from the radial and angular parts; radial and angular nodes}]
The wave function for an electron in H-like atom is given as $\psi(r,\theta,\phi)=\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2\pi}}\cdot\left(\dfrac{Z}{a_0}\right)^{5/2}\cdot r\cdot e^{-Zr/2a_0}\cdot\cos\theta$. The correct information(s) about this electron is/are -
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{It belongs to a 2p orbital}
\opt{B}{This orbital has no radial node}
\opt{C}{It belongs to a 3p orbital}
\opt{D}{Total nodes for the given orbital is 1.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TOAS12-P1-CHEM-S1-Q10, source={TOAS - Test 12 (10 Jul 2022)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=multi, subtopic={Bohr model}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K2 S2 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: photoelectric effect, hydrogen spectrum | steps: photon energy from the work function and kinetic energy; hydrogen transition; change in angular momentum; kinetic energy at the collector}]
Light from a discharge tube containing hydrogen atom fall on the surface of a piece of sodium. The kinetic energy of a fastest photo electron emitted from sodium is 0.73 eV and work function for sodium is 1.82 eV. Collector plate is connected to $+$ve terminal of battery having voltage 2 volts. Which of the following are true regarding above experiment :
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The energy of photon causing the photoelectric effect is 2.55 eV.}
\opt{B}{Hydrogen atoms electron undergoes a transition from $n=4$ to $n=2$ to show given photoelectric effect.}
\opt{C}{Change in angular momentum of the electron in the hydrogen atom will be $h/\pi$.}
\opt{D}{Kinetic energy of photoelectron at emitter plate will be 0.73 eV and at collector plate will be 2.73 eV.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\opt{D}{The orbital angular momentum of an electron in an atom is given as $\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
